blocks.text: Diabetic neuropathy refers to a group of nerve disorders caused by diabetes mellitus, resulting from chronic metabolic and microvascular injury to peripheral and autonomic nerves.
Diabetic foot disease refers to infection, ulceration or destruction of foot tissues associated with peripheral neuropathy and/or peripheral arterial disease in a person with diabetes.
It is a major cause of preventable lower-limb amputation.
**A. Diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN)**
This is the commonest form, usually presenting as distal symmetrical polyneuropathy.

items.text: Begins in the toes and feet.
Progresses proximally in a stocking distribution.
May eventually involve the hands in a glove distribution.
Causes sensory loss, pain and sometimes motor dysfunction.

blocks.text: **B. Diabetic autonomic neuropathy**
Affects autonomic nervous system function.

rows: Resting tachycardia, postural hypotension, silent myocardial ischaemia
Erectile dysfunction, bladder dysfunction, urinary retention
Reduced sweating, dry skin, altered sweating

blocks.text: **C. Diabetic mononeuropathy**
Involves an individual nerve or nerve group.
**D. Diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy**
Also called diabetic amyotrophy.

items.text: Severe proximal thigh or hip pain.
Difficulty walking or rising from a chair.

rows: Foot complications predominantly due to sensory and motor neuropathy

Management has two major components: treatment of diabetic neuropathy and prevention or treatment of diabetic foot complications.

blocks.text: Good glycaemic control reduces the risk of developing diabetic neuropathy and can slow progression, particularly in type 1 diabetes.
Glycaemic control does not reliably reverse established nerve damage. Pain control and prevention of further injury remain essential.

subsections.subsection_title: 6. Antibiotic treatment of diabetic foot infections

blocks.text: Antimicrobial stewardship
Antibiotics are indicated for clinically infected diabetic foot ulcers, not for every ulcer.
A clinically uninfected ulcer should not receive antibiotics simply to prevent infection or promote healing.

blocks.text: Diabetic foot osteomyelitis is infection of the bones of the foot, usually occurring by direct extension from a chronic ulcer.
Selected patients may be managed without surgery, particularly those with forefoot osteomyelitis, no significant PAD, no exposed bone and no immediate need for drainage.
Antibiotics should be guided by bone or deep-tissue microbiology where possible.
**Duration:** Usually six weeks when infected bone has not been resected.
The choice depends on the extent of infection, vascular supply and likelihood of functional healing.

Charcot neuroarthropathy is a progressive inflammatory and destructive condition affecting bones, joints and soft tissues of the foot and ankle in patients with peripheral neuropathy.
It results in joint instability, fractures, dislocations and deformity.
Treat suspected active Charcot foot urgently
The most important immediate intervention is immobilisation and offloading.
**Management principles**

items.text: Use a non-removable knee-high device where appropriate.
Reduce weight-bearing and use mobility aids.
Refer to a specialist diabetic foot or orthopaedic service.
Monitor resolution of inflammation and progression of deformity.
Consider surgery for severe deformity, instability or recurrent ulceration.

blocks.text: **Important:** Do not mistake an acutely inflamed Charcot foot for cellulitis or DVT. These conditions can also coexist.
Antibiotics are not indicated for Charcot neuroarthropathy alone in the absence of infection.
Amputation is considered when limb preservation is no longer possible or would create unacceptable risk to life.
